\chapter{The Meal}
\label{ch:ml-the-meal}
\hlchaptermodality{40}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say I am having a meal in Malayalam, using a second eat-verb this book never taught until now, and close the polite-request-and-repair stretch that dayavaayi opened eight chapters ago.}

Say njaan oon unnunnu against Chapter 32's tinnunnu, say enikku oon ishtamaanu on Chapter 6's dative and Chapter 34's frame, and name kshamikkanam as the repair half of the spine node dayavaayi's asking half opened.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ūṇ]{\ml{ഊണ്} (ūṇ) — \textquotedblleft{}a meal,\textquotedblright{} the word that closes this stretch's table}

\label{lesson:ML-C40-oon}



\begin{quote}
An earlier chapter taught \textbf{\ml{തിന്നുക}}, \textquotedblleft{}to eat,\textquotedblright{} for anything at all. It never taught the word for a proper, sit-down meal. Here it is.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഊണ്}} — \emph{ūṇ} — \textbf{a meal}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{ഊണ്} \ml{ഉണ്ണുന്നു}.} — \emph{ñān ūṇ uṇṇunnu.} — \textquotedblleft{}I am having a meal.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{ഊ}} is the \textbf{independent} long‑\emph{ū} vowel — the shape a word uses when it \emph{opens} with this sound and there is no consonant in front of it to carry the small sign \textbf{\ml{ൂ}} instead. It is the same kind of independent vowel letter as the very first inherent‑\emph{a} opening; the sound only changes shape depending on what, if anything, comes before it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{ഊണ്}} is native Dravidian, sharing its root with the verb \textbf{\ml{ഉണ്ണുക}} (\emph{uṇṇuka}), \textquotedblleft{}to eat a meal\textquotedblright{} — a second eat-verb this book has never taught, standing beside the everyday \textbf{\ml{തിന്നുക}}. The difference is the same one English makes between \textquotedblleft{}eating\textquotedblright{} in general and \textquotedblleft{}having a meal\textquotedblright{}: \emph{tinnuka} covers a snack, a fruit, anything at all; \emph{uṇṇuka} names sitting down to the real thing.

Tamil's cognate \textbf{\ta{உணவு}} (\emph{uṇavu}) generalised the very same root all the way to \textquotedblleft{}food\textquotedblright{} itself. Kannada's \textbf{\ml{ഊട}} (\emph{ūṭa}) narrowed it to \textquotedblleft{}a meal,\textquotedblright{} matching Malayalam's own \textbf{\ml{ഊണ്}} sense for sense — three sisters, one Proto-Dravidian root, three different landing points.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the stretch this chapter closes}]
\textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{ഊണ്} \ml{ഇഷ്ടമാണ്}.} — \emph{enikku ūṇ iṣṭamāṇŭ.} — \textquotedblleft{}I like having a meal\textquotedblright{} — the familiar dative \textbf{‑ikku}, the \emph{iṣṭaṁ} liking-frame, one more turn of the same machine.

This chapter closes the spine node \textbf{\ml{ദയവായി}} opened: \textbf{\ml{ദയവായി}} asks; \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}} repairs, the word for showing up after the \textbf{\ml{ഊണ്}} is already over. And \textbf{‑ikku} is still the same cousin of Tamil's \textbf{‑ukku}, Telugu's \textbf{‑ku}, and Kannada's \textbf{‑ge} that was first named earlier in this book.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ñān ūṇ uṇṇunnu\textquotedblright{} — I am having a meal
  \item everyday against a proper meal — \textquotedblleft{}tinnunnu … uṇṇunnu\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}enikku ūṇ iṣṭamāṇŭ\textquotedblright{} — I like having a meal
  \item ask, then repair — \textquotedblleft{}dayavāyi … kṣamikkaṇaṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item this chapter's three drinks and its meal — \textquotedblleft{}chāya, kāppi, pāl … ūṇ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I am having a meal.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ñān ūṇ uṇṇunnu}.) How does \emph{uṇṇuka} differ from the everyday \emph{tinnuka}? (\emph{Tinnuka} is \textbf{eating in general}; \emph{uṇṇuka} is \textbf{having a proper meal}.) What are the two halves this spine node runs between? (\textbf{\ml{ദയവായി}} asks; \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}} repairs.)
